newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Manuel presents first budget Wednesday.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Manuel presents first budget Wednesday.

text.p: South African Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, who presents the ruling ANC's first budget on Wednesday, has moved as smoothly from command to market economics as he has from blue jeans to black tie.

Manuel, 41, made his name in community politics among Cape Town's textile workers, fighting for civic rights and home ownership denied to the region's majority mixed-race coloured population under apartheid.

He was detained without trial repeatedly between 1986 and 1989, once for over two years, and took part in a prison hunger strike that helped to halt the National Party's bid to crush black revolt in the last years of white rule.
"Trevor has never been afraid of a fight - not on the streets then or in the cabinet now," says one colleague in President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress (ANC) government.

Now the big fists that split many a lip in clashes with right-wingers and police more often sign off on billion rand budget lines or deftly knot a black bow tie as he tours the capitals of the global economy South Africa seeks to join.
His trademark motorbike and beret have made way for a BMW limousine and, occasionally, Concorde.

Manuel, who has no formal education beyond high school, is strongly criticised by ANC idealogues for moving away from the command economy that the party initially espoused to the market-driven economy he now advocates.

He clashed head-on with the powerful Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) over the macro-economic strategy for growth, employment and redistribution, known as GEAR, which he released in June last year, but refused to bend.
The strategy commits the government to cutting the budget deficit from 5.1 percent in 1996/97 to four percent in this week's budget and to three percent by 1999.

In a mix hailed by investors abroad and the IMF, his strategy proposes full or partial privatisation of state assets, gradual dismantling of exchange controls, price and wage restraint, labour flexibility and public spending cuts to achieve growth of six percent by the turn of the century.
Manuel defended his stance in a recent interview, saying that South Africa could not succeed unless it recognised the imperative of the global economy.
"It's out there. It's real. We've got to understand what its about and work it," he said.

Manuel was assigned to the economic front line in 1992, when the ANC made him head of the economic policy desk preparing the liberation movement allowed back from exile in 1990 for the power it assumed in April 1994.
In an early interview with Reuters, in which he insisted the ANC would never abandon nationalisation, he acknowledged that he was on "a vertical learning curve."

Mandela named him minister of trade and industry in the first all-race cabinet in 1994, but switched him to finance when non-partisan white banker Chris Liebenberg resigned two weeks after presenting the 1996/97 budget last March.
Manuel won respect at home and abroad for his tough review of trade policy, including drastic tariff-cutting and plans to promote competition among the country's big corporations.
Now, as he refines his first budget speech, Manuel has the respect, or at least the ear, of most investors and economists.
"As yet, he is an unproven quantity...people will be watching very closely," said Avril Stassen, chief investor for Southern Asset Management.
"If you think about how far they have come in the past five years, from nationalisation to privatisation, it's quite a mind shift. This is an important budget to see what they offer."

Stassen recalled Manuel's occasional gaffes, including a damaging reference to "amorphous markets" whose influence should be ignored, adding: "He has continued to make that sort of utterance - that he won't be dictated to by the markets.

"I don't think he has had an opportunity to redeem the damage he did early on in his term. Maybe this budget will be the opportunity for people to decide whether he has got the capability to be a successful minister of finance," he said.
Old Mutual chief economist Dave Mohr was less cautious, saying he would give Manuel seven out of 10 so far.
"Given the change in fiscal policy that we have seen over the past few months, he certainly has learned a lot.
"We've had some rather unfortunate public comments, but we haven't heard any of them of late. So I take that as another indicator that he has learned on the job," Mohr said.
